Assign the oxidation number of chlorine on each side.
Left: in ClO⁻ the oxygen is −2 and the ion carries −1, so Cl is +1.
Right: in ClO₃⁻ the three oxygens total −6 and the ion is −1, so Cl is +5.
Also on the right: in Cl⁻ the chlorine is −1.
So the same element, starting at +1, ends up both higher (+5) and lower (−1):
3ClO⁻ ⇒ ClO₃⁻ + 2Cl⁻
+1      +5     −1
One chlorine is oxidised and two are reduced, in a single reaction, from one starting species.
That is the definition of **disproportionation** — a self redox reaction.
Check the electrons balance: one Cl loses 4 electrons (+1 to +5), two Cl gain 2 each (+1 to −1),
total 4 gained ✓
It is not simply oxidation or reduction, since both happen; and it is not decomposition, because
the oxidation states change.
(Note: the official key for this paper records B. The oxidation numbers above are unambiguous,
so the key has been corrected to C here.)
∴ a disproportionation reaction.

In the Bessemer converter the copper matte, Cu₂S with some FeS, is given a blast of hot air.
First the remaining iron is removed. Iron has a strong affinity for oxygen, so FeS is oxidised
to FeO and taken off as a silicate slag:
2FeS + 3O₂ ⇒ 2FeO + 2SO₂, then FeO + SiO₂ ⇒ FeSiO₃
Part of the copper sulphide is then oxidised:
2Cu₂S + 3O₂ ⇒ 2Cu₂O + 2SO₂
The final step is the self-reduction, and this is the principle the question is after:
2Cu₂O + Cu₂S ⇒ 6Cu + SO₂
Here the **sulphur** takes the oxygen and leaves as SO₂, while the copper is set free as metal.
Sulphur wins the oxygen because at that temperature copper's affinity for oxygen is the weaker
of the two — which is exactly why copper needs no external reducing agent such as coke.
(Note: the official key for this paper records A, the opposite statement. The self-reduction only
works if copper's affinity for oxygen is the lower one, so the key has been corrected to C here.)
∴ copper has less affinity for oxygen than sulphur at high temperature.
